title: From New to Second-Hand: Consumer Trade-offs Between Price, Range and Vehicle Condition for BEVs and Hybrids in Australia
affiliations: The University of Sydney and The University of Sydney

detail.title: From New to Second-Hand: Consumer Trade-offs Between Price, Range and Vehicle Condition for BEVs and Hybrids in Australia
detail.abstract: Most empirical work on vehicle choice has focused on new-vehicle purchase decisions, even though households often acquire vehicles through the second-hand market and face a different set of constraints and information conditions. This paper addresses that gap by estimating a single choice framework that spans new and second-hand passenger vehicle markets, allowing direct comparison of how consumers value vehicle attributes and how substitution patterns differ across the two segments. We use a discrete choice experiment administered to a New South Wales sample, with alternatives that include new and second-hand vehicles and an opt-out, and attributes that reflect both markets, including purchase price, body type, vehicle size, powertrain, range, delivery availability for new vehicles, and odometer and condition for second-hand vehicles. Preferences are estimated using a two-class latent class model with error components to capture correlation in unobserved utility and segment-specific substitution within new and second-hand markets. The results show substantial heterogeneity in valuations and clear differences between new and second-hand decision processes, with second-hand quality signals exerting economically meaningful effects and price sensitivity being stronger for second-hand choices. Powertrain attributes matter, but their implications vary by market segment and by class, indicating that technology preferences interact with the institutional and informational features of the market in which the vehicle is acquired. Applying the estimated class-membership model to population microdata, we generate conditional parameter and willingness-to-pay distributions for a large synthetic population and predict market shares for simulated vehicle profiles. The simulation results underscore that secondary-market dynamics materially shape predicted demand patterns, which has implications for policies and market designs that aim to influence fleet composition through interventions that operate in, or propagate through, the second-hand market.

title: Do Low Emission Zones generate car fleet renewal? A quasi-natural experiment

detail.title: Do Low Emission Zones generate car fleet renewal? A quasi-natural experiment
detail.abstract: This study evaluates whether the introduction of Low Emission Zones accelerates car fleet renewal. To achieve this aim, this study uses the 2017 introduction of the Ultra Low Emission Zone in London, United Kingdom. This policy required drivers of older cars (Euro 4 or older) to pay a £10 charge per day to enter a specific area of central London. A spatial difference-in-differences empirical design is implemented to estimate the causal impact of the policy.  Findings of the analysis are that the introduction of this policy increased vehicle fleet renewal by 2.2%. A practical use of this finding is that such ancillary benefits can now be included in the business case development for such policies, quantifying the broader spectrum of positive outcomes that can be realised.

title: Secrecy culture, creditor rights, and corporate cash holdings Barbara Abou Tanos [[EQUATION]]  Neveen Ahmed [[EQUATION]]  Omar Farooq [[EQUATION]]  Mohamed Shaban [[EQUATION]]
affiliations: American University of Beirut, American University of Beirut, The American University in Cairo and University of Leicester

detail.title: Secrecy culture, creditor rights, and corporate cash holdings Barbara Abou Tanos [[EQUATION]]  Neveen Ahmed [[EQUATION]]  Omar Farooq [[EQUATION]]  Mohamed Shaban [[EQUATION]]
detail.abstract: This study examines how secrecy culture influences the relationship between creditor rights and cash holdings. We analyze data from non-financial firms in 36 emerging markets using various methods. Our results reveal that firms in secretive cultures demonstrate a weaker association between creditor rights and cash holdings. The results indicate that the inherent information asymmetries in secrecy cultures hinder the enforcement of creditor rights. Consequently, when enforcement is limited, firms have less incentive to accumulate cash in response to strong creditor rights, which reduces the positive impact of creditor rights on cash holdings. Our findings are consistent and robust across various estimation methods, sub-samples, and alternative definitions of secrecy culture and cash holdings. Our results emphasize the importance of integrating cultural factors into policies that promote transparency and financial stability. Such an approach can counteract the adverse impacts that specific cultural norms may have on the effectiveness of law enforcement and governance.

title: Analysis of global city connectivity by air transport considering weighted and directed networks

detail.title: Analysis of global city connectivity by air transport considering weighted and directed networks
detail.abstract: City centrality in air transport depends on whether connectivity is measured by true origin-destination demand or by flown legs. Using ticketing itineraries and passenger volumes aggregated at city level, we build three directed weighted networks: final-destination, decoupled-leg (flown segments), and non-stop (direct services). We compute degree, strength, reciprocity, efficiency, and betweenness, and define passenger-weighted betweenness as the share of origin-destination passengers whose itinerary is routed through each transfer city. Topological indicators are representation-sensitive: the final-destination network yields much higher effective connectivity, revealing reachability enabled by hub routing, whereas leg and non-stop networks expose the operational hub-and-spoke structure. By contrast, normalized strength distributions are nearly invariant, implying a robust hierarchy of passenger volumes. Structural betweenness is a useful proxy for transfer roles but does not deterministically predict flow-mediated intermediacy. We propose a composite index combining connectivity, flow intensity, connecting traffic, and intermediacy; the core-set is the top 30 cities under an equal-weight specification, and the quasi-core comprises non-core cities dominant in one dimension. Alternative weights are used only as robustness checks. The framework yields a compact descriptor of the global city skeleton and separates routing-enabled reachability from direct services.

title: Disability Employment Quotas: Effects of Laws and Nudges
affiliations: Inter-American Development Bank, Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile and

detail.title: Disability Employment Quotas: Effects of Laws and Nudges
detail.abstract: We study Chile’s 2019 disability employment quota using linked employment and disability records. The quota increases the share of workers with disabilities (PwD) in eligible firms by 14% and the number of PwD per firm by 23%, largely through reclassification but also through some new hiring. It does not harm firms on productivity-related measures such as wages, employment, or survival. Nationally, the policy translates into a 4.2% increase in PwD employment. PwD face substantial baseline disadvantages, and the reform modestly improves their likelihood of employment, especially for younger workers and those with sensory or physical disabilities. A large-scale letters experiment shows that informational nudges primarily raise PwD employment through reclassification, while information on fines prompts small hiring increases, although overall compliance indicators don’t change. The study provides evidence on labor inclusion and firm productivity effects of disability quotas in a middle-income context, evaluates quota impacts beyond enforcement, and tests a low-cost information intervention as a potential tool to strengthen compliance.

title: Gendered Effects of Children on Well-Being and Labor Supply: Evidence from Intended Parenthood after IVF
affiliations: Federal Institute for Population Research and University of Basel

detail.title: Gendered Effects of Children on Well-Being and Labor Supply: Evidence from Intended Parenthood after IVF
detail.abstract: We assess the gendered effects of having children on well-being, labor supply, and the division of domestic work. We exploit plausibly exogenous variation in parenthood generated by in-vitro fertilization (IVF) treatments. Children increase mothers’ well-being only temporarily, while fathers experience more persistent gains. Only mothers exhibit a lasting reduction in labor supply and a sustained increase in domestic work. At the same time, mothers' satisfaction with the division of labor declines, and they are more likely to perceive it as unfair. Because our analysis focuses on relatively affluent individuals with a strong desire for children, the results need not generalize to all parents. Within this population, however, we document persistent gender asymmetries in the distribution of time costs and well-being gains from parenthood. These patterns are relevant for the design of family and labor market policies and could help explain declining fertility in many Western countries, where anticipated post-childbirth inequalities could deter childbearing.

title: Impact of Wind-Assistance on the Efficiency of a Tramp Fleet

detail.title: Impact of Wind-Assistance on the Efficiency of a Tramp Fleet
detail.abstract: Wind-assisted ship propulsion (WASP) is expected to be an important element of the shipping decarbonization. However, studying WASP for a single vessel may neglect its full potential compared to planning a fleet of vessels as a whole. We therefore extend a fleet routing optimization model with weather-dependent routing. The optimization model includes speed optimization, bunkering, charter costs, and the spot market, thereby enabling greater WASP benefits. Historical freight rates and bunker prices are used in the experiments. The results show that profits can be 5% higher using WASP within the same emission envelope. Moreover, in a multi-criteria setting, it is seen that 30-40% reductions in emissions can be achieved while maintaining constant profit. Finally, our experiments show that the fleet-oriented approach can achieve twice the emission reduction achieved by the vessel-oriented approach, indicating that WASP is an important measure for meeting the IMO’s emission goals.

title: Persuasion in Physician Agency
affiliations: , University of Bologna and University of York - Department of Economics and Related Studies

detail.title: Persuasion in Physician Agency
detail.abstract: We analyze the physician–patient agency problem in a setting where patients have heterogeneous treatment preferences and physicians choose which diagnostic test to administer. Due to imperfect test accuracy, the equilibrium features both undertreatment and overtreatment. We assess the health and welfare effects of three policy interventions: improving test accuracy, imposing a minimum accuracy standard, and mandating testing. Enhancing test accuracy can reduce both undertreatment and unnecessary care, thereby improving health outcomes and welfare under certain conditions. A minimum accuracy standard can reduce overtreatment by eliminating tests with high false-positive rates, but may also increase undertreatment if the excluded tests are valuable for identifying sick patients. The net health impact depends on the trade-off between the specificity and sensitivity of the remaining test. Mandating testing improves health outcomes for high-preference patients by avoiding unnecessary treatment, but its welfare effects are mixed, as the added testing costs yield no benefit for low-preference patients who remain untreated.

title: Cost-Effective and Low-Carbon Cooling Strategies for Data Centers Integrated into Wind Turbine Towers
affiliations: Paderborn University, Paderborn University, Paderborn University and Paderborn University

detail.title: Cost-Effective and Low-Carbon Cooling Strategies for Data Centers Integrated into Wind Turbine Towers
detail.abstract: In the pursuit of sustainable and energy-efficient data center (DC) infrastructure, using renewable energy sources to supply DCs is a promising solution. This paper presents an integrated design that (1) proposes a comprehensive model for utilizing the wind turbine tower (WTT) structure for efficient and potentially passive cooling, and (2) harnesses curtailed wind energy (CWE) that would otherwise remain unused. Building on this concept, this paper develops an optimization model for the design and operation of a cooling system for a DC built in a WTT. The model aims to minimize both total system costs and carbon emissions by evaluating three cooling strategies: (1) utilizing the WTT as a heat exchanger for heat dissipation to the environment, (2) implementing free cooling, and (3) deploying compressor chillers, either individually or in combination. The model employs a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming framework and addresses uncertainties in weather conditions, electricity prices, CWE, and carbon emission factors. Through a detailed simulation case study, the proposed approach demonstrates significant improvements of the assumed system compared to a system without WTT-based cooling and CWE utilization, achieving 7.3–12.92% cost savings and a 15.23–18.72% reduction in CO2 emissions. WTT cooling’s contribution increases consistently with DC return temperature, ranging from 1.33% to nearly 7.31%. Additionally, 73.4% of the available CWE is effectively utilized: 62.6% for powering DC operations and 10.8% for the cooling systems.

title: When Leaders Become the Team: Support Congruence, Downward Identification, and Unethical Pro-Team Behavior
affiliations: Southern Illinois University Carbondale, Southern Illinois University Carbondale and

detail.title: When Leaders Become the Team: Support Congruence, Downward Identification, and Unethical Pro-Team Behavior
detail.abstract: Leadership research has primarily conceptualized identification as a top-down process through which leaders shape followers’ self-concepts. This study introduces downward identification, a bottom-up identity process through which leaders incorporate their teams into their self-concepts based on shared relational meaning. Drawing on social identity and relational theories, downward identification is proposed to emerge when leaders’ perceptions of support from team members align with team members’ perceptions of leader support, stabilizing relational cues into identity-relevant meaning and rendering team outcomes psychologically self-relevant for leaders. The ethical implications of downward identification are also examined. Downward identification is argued to moralize loyalty to the team, increasing leaders’ willingness to engage in unethical pro-team behavior—norm-violating actions intended to benefit the team. Importantly, this process is theorized to be contingent on teams’ organizational identification. Rather than uniformly constraining unethical conduct, high team organizational identification elevates the team as a legitimate organizational referent, shaping how leaders interpret the appropriateness of team-serving actions and amplifying the ethical consequences of downward identification. These arguments are tested using multi-source, two-wave data from 104 riot police teams in South Korea. Polynomial regression and response surface analysis indicate that leader–team support congruence predicts leaders’ downward identification, which mediates the relationship between support congruence and unethical pro-team behavior. This indirect effect is stronger when teams’ organizational identification is high. The findings advance leadership theory by reframing identification as a relational, bottom-up process and by highlighting its dual-edged ethical consequences in leadership contexts.

title: Building Business Relationships: Does the Intensity of Environmental Factors Influence Outcomes?
affiliations: Harbin University of Commerce, Harbin University of Commerce, ,  and

detail.title: Building Business Relationships: Does the Intensity of Environmental Factors Influence Outcomes?
detail.abstract: The environmental factors influencing the establishment and maintenance of business relationships are multifaceted, necessitating a comprehensive examination of these variables. This paper investigates the impact of environmental factors, specifically business ethics and etiquette, on the performance of business relationships within the context of relationship formation and posits three hypotheses for analysis. The research findings demonstrate that multiple environmental factors significantly influence business relationship performance, with business ethics and etiquette being the most critical elements. Furthermore, entities that prioritize Confucian dynamism, trust, commitment, along with business ethics and etiquette, tend to outperform those that do not emphasize these aspects in establishing and maintaining business relationships. Through regression analysis of survey data from 3,571 respondents globally, this study elucidates specific impacts between environmental factors and business relationship performance, offering theoretical insights for organizations to identify key factors for successful collaboration. This understanding aids in the formulation of more effective strategies and informed decision-making.

title: Advanced Fuzzy Decision Analytics for Medical Device Manufacturer Selection Using Complex Fermatean picture fuzzy Structures and CRITIC-TOPSIS model
affiliations: Anhui University of Chinese Medicine, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology, University of Shanghai for Science and Technology and Southwest University

detail.title: Advanced Fuzzy Decision Analytics for Medical Device Manufacturer Selection Using Complex Fermatean picture fuzzy Structures and CRITIC-TOPSIS model
detail.abstract: In modern healthcare, selecting the most appropriate medical device is a vital decision that directly influences the quality of patient care, the accuracy of diagnoses, and the overall efficiency of medical services. Given the large number of available manufacturers and the complexity of evaluation criteria, decision-makers face significant uncertainty when selecting optimal suppliers. To address this challenge, this study develops a novel decision-making framework based on complex Fermatean picture fuzzy sets, which allows for the effective handling of uncertainty and vagueness in multi-criteria decision-making scenarios. Within this framework, Frank t-norm and t-conorm operators are employed to construct a series of aggregation operators, including Frank weighted average, Frank ordered weighted average, Frank weighted geometric, and Frank ordered weighted geometric operators. These operators to confirm important properties such as idempotency and monotonicity, ensuring their application to decision-making situations. To facilitate robust decision-making, a hybrid CRITIC–TOPSIS method is integrated with the complex Fermatean picture fuzzy framework, enabling the determination of criteria weights and ranking of alternatives even when the relative importance of criteria and expert opinions are uncertain or incomplete. This integrated approach is utilized in a real-world case study for the selection of healthcare tools, highlighting its practicality and efficacy. A comparative examination with existing approaches validates the superior accuracy and adaptability of the suggested strategy. According to recent studies, these operators are highly effective in supporting decision-makers to select optimal suppliers and develop strategic, sustainable procurement policies, highlighting their potential as a valuable tool in healthcare supply chain management.

title: Integrating Two-stage Adaptive Reinforcement Learning with Differential Evolution for Dynamic Scheduling in Automated Material Handling System
affiliations: Hunan University, Jihua Laboratory, Jihua Laboratory, Jihua Laboratory and Jihua Laboratory

detail.title: Integrating Two-stage Adaptive Reinforcement Learning with Differential Evolution for Dynamic Scheduling in Automated Material Handling System
detail.abstract: As the semiconductor manufacturing industry moves towards higher precision and larger-scale production, the Automated Material Handling System (AMHS) has become a critical determinant of chip production costs, manufacturing cycle times, and product yields. The AMHS is an indispensable core automated facility in modern wafer fabs. The scheduling system is the "control center" of the AMHS, which contains the characteristics of large-scale operations, stringent real-time requirements, conflicting objectives, significant stochasticity, and frequent dynamic disturbances. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel dynamic scheduling model, which is called Two-stage Adaptive Reinforcement-Learning-Assisted Differential Evolution (TA-RLDE) scheduling algorithm, for optimizing the task allocation of overhead hoist transport (OHT) vehicles in the AMHS of semiconductor manufacturing workshops. In TA-RLDE, a two-stage RL algorithm designed to assist in optimizing the offspring individuals generated by the DE algorithm; an adaptive individual elimination and generation strategy that cooperates with the RL mechanism to balance exploration and exploitation; and a random best-matched value (RBMV) encoding/decoding strategy that enables effective mapping between the continuous and discrete scheduling domains. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared with other scheduling approaches, TA-RLDE achieves a significant reduction in the average transport time, cycle time, and waiting times of the AMHS, thereby increasing wafer throughput. Consequently, the TA-RLDE algorithm proposed in this paper enables the coordinated optimization of AMHS operations, and has important theoretical significance and engineering value for improving the overall operational efficiency of the system and reducing operational costs.

title: The Potential of Cost-Optimal Demand-Side Flexibility in Pharmaceutical Industry Clusters
affiliations: Empa, Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology, Swiss Federal Laboratories for Material Science and Technology (EMPA) and Swiss Federal Laboratories for Material Science and Technology (EMPA)

detail.title: The Potential of Cost-Optimal Demand-Side Flexibility in Pharmaceutical Industry Clusters
detail.abstract: The contribution of the industrial sector to reach climate and energy efficiency targets is essential. One technique that allows higher penetration of renewable electricity generation in the grid is demand-side management (DSM). Additional benefits from DSM include the economic benefit for the consumer, which is to profit from low electricity prices, and the better utilization of the existing infrastructure. However, the potential demand response from industry in general, and from the pharmaceutical industry in particular is still unexplored. The present study approaches this research gap by implementing a mathematical formulation of load-shifting to the district energy system modeling tool EhubX [1]. With this novel model, a real-world pharmaceutical cluster is analyzed. The results show that with day-ahead refrigeration and compressor load scheduling at selected industrial sites, electricity costs can be cut by 1.5% to 9%. However, a business case for the companies and the corresponding regulations must be implemented to exploit this potential.
